findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if a worker is slow, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering decoded results in memory without bound, which can OOM the consumer and also inflates offset-tracking state. A bounded queue plus raising `MessageRejected` (or blocking put) is needed to get the advertised backpressure.

findings.title: queue_pool is created once per factory and destroyed by strategy close(), breaking rebalances
findings.body: The `FixedQueuePool` (and its worker threads and `OffsetTracker`) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops all worker threads and shuts down the queues. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after every rebalance/partition revocation. On the second call, `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes (the attribute isn't cleared by the strategy), so a new strategy is built on top of dead workers and already-shutdown queues: submitted work is never processed and offsets are never committed, stalling the consumer silently. Additionally the `OffsetTracker`'s `last_committed`/`all_offsets` are carried across assignments, so stale per-partition state can suppress commits (or commit offsets for partitions no longer owned) after a rebalance. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or reset on revocation).

findings.title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread
findings.body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callback passed to `create_with_partitions`. That callback (and the underlying consumer offset staging) is expected to be invoked from the main processing thread; calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor's `poll`/`submit`/commit handling is not thread-safe and can corrupt or lose staged offsets. Offsets should be collected by the worker threads and flushed from `poll()` on the main thread instead.

findings.title: close() does not flush remaining committable offsets or drain queues
findings.body: `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and shuts the pool down. The commit loop exits as soon as the event is set, so any work completed in the last interval (and any work the workers finish during their 5s join) is never committed. Queued-but-unprocessed items are also dropped by `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`? they are drained only if workers keep up within the join timeout. On every consumer shutdown/rebalance this causes re-delivery (duplicate processing) of up to a second's worth of already-processed results, and silently dropped work if workers don't finish. A final `get_committable_offsets()`/commit after draining is needed.

findings.title: queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13+
findings.body: `queue.ShutDown` and `queue.Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were only added in Python 3.13. On any older interpreter this module raises `AttributeError` at worker-exception handling time and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` logs "Error shutting down queue" for every queue while workers stay blocked in `get()` forever, so the consumer can never shut down. If the runtime is not guaranteed to be 3.13+, this needs a compatibility path (e.g. sentinel items).

findings.title: Decode/grouping failures mark the offset complete and are silently dropped
findings.body: In `submit()`, any exception from the decoder or `grouping_fn` is caught, logged, and the offset is immediately added+completed, i.e. the message is committed as if processed. There is no DLQ handling and no metric, so malformed or unexpected payloads are permanently lost with only a log line. Consider routing these to the DLQ (raise `InvalidMessage`) or at least emitting a counter.

findings.title: Per-partition lock map and defaultdicts mutated without a global lock
findings.body: `_get_partition_lock` and the `defaultdict` accesses in `add_offset`/`get_committable_offsets` mutate `self.partition_locks`, `self.all_offsets` and `self.outstanding` from multiple worker threads plus the commit thread with no guarding lock (the per-partition lock is acquired only after the dict lookup/creation). This relies entirely on CPython dict/`setdefault` atomicity and will break under free-threaded builds or if the implementation changes. A single mutex guarding the maps (or a lock around lock-creation) would make the invariants explicit.

findings.title: hash() of group key is not stable across processes
findings.body: `get_queue_for_group` uses builtin `hash(group_key)`, which for `str` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). The docstring claims "consistent hashing", but assignment differs between consumer processes and across restarts. This is tolerable since each process owns distinct partitions, but if ordering guarantees are ever expected to hold across processes/restarts this is wrong; use a stable hash (e.g. md5/crc32) instead.

findings.title: WorkItem retains full Kafka message for no reason
findings.body: `WorkItem.message` stores the entire arroyo `Message` (including the raw payload bytes) but is never read anywhere; partition/offset are tracked separately. With unbounded queues this doubles the memory held per queued item. Drop the field.

findings.title: Flaky assertion that 20 groups hit all 3 queues
findings.body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` based on `hash()` of 20 group keys, which is randomized per process. It is likely but not guaranteed that all three queues are hit, so this test can fail intermittently. Assert `>= 2` or seed a deterministic hash.

findings.title: join() ignores its timeout argument
findings.body: `join(timeout)` discards `timeout` and calls `close()`, which uses hard-coded 5s joins for the commit thread and each worker. With N queues this can block for N*5s during shutdown, exceeding arroyo's join timeout and triggering a forced kill mid-processing. The timeout should be honoured/budgeted across the threads.
